qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

marking_guidance: Key term/meaning (1): output per unit of input.
objective_titles: Explain the meaning of productivity

items.prompt: Identify the output and input characteristics in a labour-productivity measure stated as acceptable boxes per worker-hour.
items.canonical_answer: Acceptable boxes measure output; worker-hours measure labour input.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): acceptable boxes as output. Distinction/example (1): worker-hours as input.
objective_titles: Explain the meaning of productivity

items.prompt: Explain the error in claiming productivity doubled when output rose from 800 to 1,600 boxes and worker-hours rose from 400 to 800.
items.canonical_answer: Production doubled, but productivity stayed at 2 boxes per worker-hour. Input and output rose in the same proportion, so the output/input ratio did not rise.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): production growth mistaken for productivity growth. Boundary/test (1): both ratios equal 2 boxes per worker-hour.
objective_titles: Explain the meaning of productivity

items.prompt: Calculate labour productivity from invented weekly output of 1,000 acceptable boxes and 400 worker-hours.
items.canonical_answer: Labour productivity = output / worker-hours = 1,000 / 400 = 2.5 acceptable boxes per worker-hour.
marking_guidance: Formula/substitution (1): 1,000 / 400. Result and units (1): 2.5 acceptable boxes per worker-hour.
objective_titles: Show how productivity is measured

items.prompt: Analyse the productivity change using invented comparable output: Week 1 has 800 acceptable boxes and 400 worker-hours; Week 2 has 1,000 boxes and 500 worker-hours.
items.canonical_answer: Output rises 25%, but input hours also rise 25%. Productivity is 2 boxes per worker-hour in each week, so higher production does not demonstrate improved labour productivity.
marking_guidance: Data/pattern (1): output and hours both rise. Evidence/calculation (1): ratios both 2. Explanation/meaning (1): no productivity improvement because input rose proportionately. Limitation (1): output total alone is insufficient.
objective_titles: Show how productivity is measured

items.prompt: Explain how targeted labelling training can improve productivity when incorrect labels currently require unpacking and redoing boxes.
items.canonical_answer: Training reduces labelling errors, so less labour time is spent on rework. With comparable quality and hours, more acceptable boxes can be completed per worker-hour; the gain depends on the training addressing the actual problem.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): relevant training. Because/mechanism (2): fewer errors (1), less rework (1). Consequence (1): more acceptable output per hour under stated conditions.
objective_titles: Discuss how productivity can be improved

items.prompt: Explain why training alone may have limited effect when the workshop’s main constraint is repeated equipment failure.
items.canonical_answer: Skills do not remove the failing equipment constraint. Maintenance or replacement may be needed before workers can use their time effectively, so the intervention must match the bottleneck.
marking_guidance: Context (1): equipment failure constraint. Reason/consequence (1): skills alone do not restore reliable equipment.
objective_titles: Discuss how productivity can be improved

items.prompt: Explain how a suitable digital order-and-label system can raise output per worker-hour when staff are trained and power is reliable.
items.canonical_answer: The system retrieves matching order details without repeated entry, reducing mistakes and time spent correcting labels. With fewer delays and rework, more acceptable boxes can be completed in the same hours, subject to effective use.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): suitable IT. Mechanism (2): less repeated entry/errors (1), less rework/time loss (1). Consequence (1): more acceptable output per hour with training and reliability.
objective_titles: Explain the effect of Information Technology on productivity

items.prompt: Explain one productivity risk when new order software is introduced without training and workers duplicate entries manually.
items.canonical_answer: Unfamiliar software and duplicate entry consume worker time without creating additional usable output. Output per worker-hour may initially fall instead of rising.
marking_guidance: Context (1): lack of training/duplicate work. Reason/consequence (1): time use without additional output may lower productivity.
objective_titles: Explain the effect of Information Technology on productivity

items.prompt: Explain a possible productivity effect in an invented workplace where illness associated with HIV and AIDS causes documented process interruptions and rework during hours worked. Do not infer effects from HIV status alone.
items.canonical_answer: The stated interruptions disrupt coordination and create rework, so fewer acceptable units may be completed per worker-hour. The mechanism depends on actual illness-related disruption; effective treatment and support can limit effects, and status alone does not establish reduced productivity.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): documented illness-related disruption. Mechanism (2): interruptions (1), rework uses hours (1). Consequence (1): acceptable output per hour may fall, conditional on actual circumstances.
objective_titles: Discuss the effects of HIV and AIDS on productivity

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between production and productivity when illness-related absence reduces hours from 400 to 300 and comparable output from 800 to 600 units.
items.canonical_answer: Production falls by 200 units, but productivity remains 2 units per worker-hour. Lost hours explain lower total output here without a reduction in the measured hourly ratio.
marking_guidance: Context (1): both output and hours fall. Reason/conclusion (1): 800/400 and 600/300 both equal 2.
objective_titles: Discuss the effects of HIV and AIDS on productivity

items.prompt: Define productivity (2). Identify the output and labour input quantities needed to measure acceptable boxes per worker-hour (2). Explain an IT effect where a trained worker’s suitable system reduces order-entry errors and rework (2). Identify two distinct ways to improve productivity (2).
items.canonical_answer: Productivity is output per unit of input. Measure acceptable boxes and worker-hours in the same period. Reduced rework permits more acceptable boxes in the same time. Relevant training and reliable maintained equipment are two ways to improve productive performance.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): output (1), per unit of input (1). Separate points (2): acceptable boxes (1), worker-hours (1). Explanation (2): fewer errors/rework (1), more acceptable output in same hours (1). Identification (2): training (1), reliable maintained equipment (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented comparable workshop data: before a suitable order system and training, 800 acceptable boxes use 400 worker-hours weekly; afterwards, 1,000 boxes use 400 worker-hours. The system reduces repeated data entry and incorrect labels; power is reliable. Separately, documented illness associated with HIV and AIDS has sometimes interrupted coordination and caused rework. Health support and cross-training are proposed. HIV status alone is not evidence of reduced productivity. Describe three measurement features, including output, input and productivity (6). Explain how the IT could contribute to the measured improvement under the stated conditions (7). Discuss whether IT and training alone provide a sufficient productivity strategy given the documented health-related disruption (7).
items.canonical_answer: Output rises 800 to 1,000 acceptable boxes; hours stay 400; productivity rises 2 to 2.5 boxes per hour, a 25% gain. Suitable IT reduces repeated entry, errors and rework, making more time available for acceptable output. Training and reliable power support effective use, though the data do not isolate IT from training. Documented illness-related disruption can still impede coordination. Health support and cross-training can complement the technology; status alone establishes no loss. An integrated strategy is better supported than IT and training alone under these conditions.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): output increase (1), 800 to 1,000 detail (1); input unchanged (1), 400 hours detail (1); ratio increase (1), 2 to 2.5 units/hour detail (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): less repeated entry (1), fewer errors (1), less rework (1), released time (1), more acceptable output/hour (1), trained staff condition (1), reliable power condition (1). Both sides/judgement (7): IT/training address process errors (1), observed gain consistent (1); actual illness disruption remains (1), support/cross-training may help (1); condition no inference from status (1); judgement combined strategy (1), linked to separate constraints (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

Health support and cross-training are proposed. HIV status alone is not evidence of reduced productivity.

items.prompt: Invented matched cases with the same suitable order software. Case 1: trained workers, reliable power, health support and cross-training preserve coordination during occasional documented illness-related absence. Case 2: no software training, unreliable power and documented illness associated with HIV and AIDS cause process interruptions and rework; support and continuity arrangements are absent. No productivity totals are supplied, and HIV status alone is not evidence of reduced productivity. Evaluate the prospects for productivity improvement in Case 1 (7). Evaluate whether installing the same software alone is likely to secure the same improvement in Case 2 (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: training and reliability support fewer entry errors, while health support and cross-training preserve processes. Gains are plausible but not quantified or guaranteed. Case 2: software has potential, yet lack of training, outages and actual health-related process disruption can prevent effective use. Matching Case 1 requires addressing these constraints; no individual effect follows simply from HIV status.
marking_guidance: Case 1 allocation (7): argument for trained use (1), reliable process (1); argument against unquantified gain (1), residual disruption possible (1); condition ongoing support/continuity (1); judgement plausible improvement (1), linked to implementation (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for useful software potential (1), error-reduction mechanism (1); argument against missing skills/reliability (1), actual illness disruption (1); condition constraints addressed without status assumptions (1); judgement software alone insufficient (1), linked to complementary support (1). Total marks 14.
